title: YOU SAY YOU FOLLOW JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME OBEYING HIM ACTUALLY COST YOU SOMETHING?
paragraphs: YOU SAY YOU FOLLOW JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME OBEYING HIM ACTUALLY COST YOU SOMETHING?
The Most Dangerous Kind of Christianity Is the Kind That Calls Jesus Lord but Quietly Refuses to Follow Him When His Commands Become Uncomfortable.
There is a question that can expose more about your relationship with Jesus than a thousand worship songs, a hundred church services, or a lifetime of Christian social media posts.
And the frightening part?
You might already know the answer.
When was the last time you obeyed Jesus even though it cost you something you desperately wanted to keep?
Not when obedience was convenient.
Not when doing the right thing earned you applause.
Not when following Jesus fit comfortably into your schedule, your relationships, your finances, or your plans.
I'm talking about the moment you knew exactly what God was asking of you… and everything inside you wanted to walk in the opposite direction.
The relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ, but you couldn't imagine losing.
The apology you needed to make, even though you were convinced the other person owed you one first.
The money you could have kept by being dishonest.
The secret sin you kept returning to because nobody else knew.
The truth you were afraid to speak because you might lose someone's approval.
The forgiveness you were withholding because the wound was real, the betrayal was painful, and the person who hurt you never even said sorry.
You knew what Scripture said.
You knew what obedience required.
But you also knew what it might cost.
And somewhere between knowing God's Word and surrendering to it, you began negotiating.
"Lord, I'll follow You. Just don't ask me to give up this."
"Lord, I'll obey You. Just let me handle this one situation my way."
"Lord, You can have my future. But please don't touch the thing I'm holding right now."
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that you never stopped calling Him Lord.
You still prayed.
You still attended church.
You still shared Bible verses.
You still believed Jesus was the Son of God.
But there was a locked room in your heart where your obedience ended and your preferences began.
And Jesus knew exactly where that room was.
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" — Luke 6:46, KJV
Read that again.
Not because it's complicated.
Because it's painfully clear.
Jesus was not addressing people who had never heard of Him. He was confronting the contradiction between acknowledging His authority and refusing His instructions.
In the original Greek, the word translated "Lord" is κύριε (kyrie), a form of κύριος (kyrios), meaning lord, master, or one possessing authority.
When Jesus asks why people call Him "Lord, Lord," the repetition intensifies the profession.
Yet the problem remains.
Their mouths acknowledge His authority while their actions resist it.
And suddenly the question becomes personal.
Is Jesus truly Lord over your life, or have you quietly reduced Him to someone whose advice you follow only when you agree with it?
That question should make all of us uncomfortable.
Including the person writing these words.
Because it is possible to become so familiar with Christian language that we stop trembling at Christian truth.
We learn how to say "God is in control" while desperately protecting our own control.
We say "Your will be done" while secretly hoping His will looks exactly like ours.
We sing "I surrender all" while mentally identifying everything we refuse to surrender.
And eventually, without even noticing, we can build a version of Christianity that comforts our emotions without confronting our rebellion.
But Jesus never invited anyone into a comfortable arrangement where He receives admiration without authority.
He called people to follow Him.
And following means moving when He says move.
Even when the road leads somewhere we would never have chosen.
There was once a man who approached Jesus with a question about eternal life.
He wasn't presented as a violent criminal or an obvious enemy of God.
He was a man who took morality seriously.
He knew the commandments.
He had a respectable religious history.
And according to Mark's Gospel, something extraordinary happened when Jesus looked at him.
"Then Jesus beholding him loved him…" — Mark 10:21, KJV
Don't miss those words.
Jesus loved him.
Before confronting him.
Before exposing what was missing.
Before asking him to surrender what he treasured.
Jesus loved him.
And then came the command that uncovered the man's heart.
Jesus told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The Greek text of Mark 10:21 includes the words δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι (deuro akolouthei moi).
"Come, follow Me."
This was not a universal command requiring every Christian to sell every possession. Jesus was confronting the particular attachment that held this man captive.
His wealth had become more than something he possessed.
It was something he could not bear to release.
And then Scripture records one of the saddest departures in the Gospels.
"And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." — Mark 10:22, KJV
He came looking for eternal life.
He stood before the One who is life.
He was loved by Jesus.
And he walked away grieving because the invitation required a surrender he was unwilling to make.
Think about that.
He didn't walk away because Jesus hated him.
He walked away after being loved.
He didn't walk away because Jesus was unclear.
He walked away because Jesus was painfully clear.
And the possessions he couldn't release became the reason he turned away from the Savior standing before him.
Now ask yourself something.
What would Jesus have to ask you to surrender before you started walking away?
Would it be your reputation?
Your relationship?
Your bitterness?
Your financial security?
Your private habits?
Your desire to be admired?
Your need to win every argument?
Your carefully protected plans?
Perhaps it isn't something obviously sinful.
Perhaps it's something good that has slowly become ultimate.
Something you enjoy, something you value, something you have begun trusting more than the God who gave it.
Because an idol doesn't always look evil.
Sometimes it looks like the one thing you cannot imagine living without.
And the tragedy is not that God delights in taking things away from His children.
The tragedy is that we sometimes cling so tightly to temporary things that we resist the One who offers eternal life.
But before you start believing this article is telling you to earn God's love through painful sacrifices, we need to look at something even more important.
The Gospel is not that you must suffer enough to make Jesus accept you. The Gospel is that Jesus gave Himself for sinners who could never earn their own salvation.
Scripture says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
In the Greek text, χάριτί (chariti) comes from χάρις (charis), meaning grace.
God's saving grace is not a paycheck for impressive obedience.
It is His undeserved favor given through Jesus Christ.
You cannot purchase forgiveness with enough good deeds.
You cannot earn adoption into God's family by surrendering enough possessions.
You cannot make the cross more powerful by adding your own suffering to it.
Jesus has accomplished what you could never accomplish.
And yet the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for them to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace is not opposed to obedience.
Grace is opposed to the idea that obedience can earn salvation.
The obedience of a believer is the fruit of God's saving work, not the price of admission into His kingdom.
That's why Jesus says:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments." — John 14:15, KJV
Love does not make obedience unnecessary.
Love gives obedience its proper place.
We do not obey to persuade Jesus to love us.
We learn to obey because He first loved us.
And sometimes that obedience will cost us dearly.
Not because every painful choice is automatically holy.
Not because hardship itself proves spiritual maturity.
But because a fallen world will not always celebrate faithfulness to Christ.
And our own sinful desires will not always surrender without a fight.
There is a difference between carrying a cross and simply enduring a difficult life.
Jesus said:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." — Luke 9:23, KJV
The Greek word translated "daily" is καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath' hēmeran), meaning day by day.
Not once during an emotional altar call.
Not only when the worship music is playing.
Not merely during a season when your faith feels strong.
Daily.
When you're exhausted.
When you're misunderstood.
When you're tempted.
When obedience feels lonely.
When nobody notices your integrity.
When doing the right thing seems to produce no immediate reward.
Following Jesus is not merely a dramatic decision made in public.
It is a lifetime of surrender expressed in ordinary moments.
Sometimes the cost is refusing to participate in dishonest business practices when everyone around you calls them normal.
Sometimes it's ending a pattern of sexual sin even when you know the loneliness that may follow.
Sometimes it's admitting to your spouse that you've been hiding something and accepting responsibility instead of protecting your image.
Sometimes it's choosing not to retaliate against someone who humiliated you.
Sometimes it's returning what doesn't belong to you.
Sometimes it's refusing to compromise the truth just to remain popular.
Sometimes it's asking for help because you finally understand that pretending to be spiritually strong is not the same as walking in the light.
And sometimes the most expensive act of obedience is simply telling God the truth.
"Lord, I don't want to obey You right now."
"I know what Your Word says, but my heart is resisting."
"I'm afraid of what I'll lose."
"I need You to change what I cannot change by myself."
That prayer may not sound impressive.
But it is far more honest than pretending to surrender while secretly planning to remain in control.
And there is a man in Scripture who understood the shame of discovering that his loyalty was weaker than he believed.
His name was Peter.
Peter was bold.
Passionate.
Quick to speak.
Quick to promise.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would fall away, Peter was convinced his devotion would survive whatever came.
He declared that even if everyone else stumbled, he would not.
He was willing, he said, to die with Jesus.
And then came the courtyard.
The darkness.
The accusations.
The fear.
The moment when following Jesus no longer sounded like an inspiring promise but carried the possibility of suffering.
And Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had confidently promised to die with Jesus became afraid to admit he knew Him.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter remembered.
"And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." — Luke 22:62, KJV
Can you imagine that walk?
Leaving the courtyard.
Hearing the rooster's cry echoing in your mind.
Remembering every confident promise you made.
Knowing that when loyalty became expensive, you chose self-preservation.
Perhaps you know something about that walk.
Maybe you promised God you would never return to that sin.
But you did.
Maybe you told Him you would stop compromising.
But the pressure came, and you gave in.
Maybe you said you would speak about Jesus openly.
But when the conversation turned hostile, you stayed silent.
Maybe you told yourself your faith was stronger than your fear.
Then life tested you.
And you discovered how fragile your courage really was.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
And yours does not have to end in the place where you failed.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved Him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The three questions painfully recall Peter's three denials, although the passage does not explicitly explain the repetition in those terms.
What is unmistakable is that Jesus did not treat Peter's failure as the final word over his life.
He restored and recommissioned him.
The disciple who had denied knowing Jesus was called to follow Him again.
And this time, Jesus also spoke about the costly death Peter would eventually face (John 21:18–19).
Then He said:
"Follow me." — John 21:19, KJV
The same essential invitation.
But now Peter knew something about himself that he had not understood before.
His confidence was not enough.
His passion was not enough.
His promises were not enough.
He needed the grace of the Savior he had denied.
And that is where true obedience begins.
Not in the arrogance of saying, "Lord, I would never fail You."
But in the humility of praying, "Lord, without You, I cannot stand."
This is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not excuse our sin.
But neither does He abandon repentant sinners to the wreckage of their worst moments.
He confronts.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
And He calls us forward.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming disobedience as freedom.
Not by telling us repentance is unnecessary.
But by accomplishing redemption through His death and resurrection and bringing sinners into a new life through faith in Him.
And now we must face a difficult question.
Have we mistaken the absence of persecution for the presence of obedience?
Have we confused religious activity with spiritual surrender?
Have we learned to defend Christianity in arguments while refusing to practice Christianity in private?
Because it is possible to know the correct answer to a biblical question and still resist the biblical command standing directly in front of us.
James writes:
The Greek word translated "doers" is ποιηταί (poiētai), referring to those who put something into practice.
James is not attacking the importance of hearing God's Word.
He is warning against the self-deception of hearing without responding.
And that deception is dangerous because it can feel remarkably spiritual.
You can listen to a sermon about forgiveness and still nourish resentment.
You can study generosity while remaining controlled by greed.
You can post about holiness while protecting secret sin.
You can memorize verses about loving your neighbor while treating the people in your home with cruelty.
You can publicly defend biblical marriage while privately neglecting your spouse.
You can passionately discuss revival while refusing to repent.
And you can become so busy talking about Jesus that you stop listening when He tells you to change.
But the answer is not to abandon church, worship, Bible study, or Christian fellowship.
We need those things.
The answer is to stop using good spiritual activities as substitutes for surrendered hearts.
Jesus did not say, "Blessed are those who know the most about My commandments."
He said:
"If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them." — John 13:17, KJV
And the setting matters.
Jesus had just washed His disciples' feet.
The Lord and Teacher had taken the position of a servant.
The One who deserved honor stooped to serve those who could never repay Him.
So perhaps the obedience God is calling you to today isn't dramatic enough to impress anyone.
Perhaps it looks like washing the dishes when you're tired.
Listening patiently when you want to defend yourself.
Serving someone who cannot advance your reputation.
Speaking gently to a child after a long day.
Confessing a lie.
Keeping a promise.
Praying for someone who wounded you.
Showing mercy without surrendering healthy boundaries or excusing ongoing abuse.
Refusing to turn another person's weakness into gossip.
Or doing the right thing when you know no one on earth will ever find out.
Heaven does not measure faithfulness by how impressive it looks on a screen.
God sees what is done in secret.
And some of the most meaningful acts of obedience will never become public testimonies.
They will simply be known to the Father.
But there is another danger we must confront.

Some people will read a message about costly obedience and immediately think they must prove their devotion by staying in an abusive relationship, tolerating exploitation, giving away money they need for basic responsibilities, or remaining silent when someone harms them.
That is not what Scripture requires.
Following Jesus does not mean enabling evil.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for justice, repentance, safety, or wise boundaries.
Generosity is not permission for religious leaders to manipulate the vulnerable.
And no human being has the right to demand blind obedience under the claim that they speak for God.
Christian obedience must be measured against the truth of Scripture and the character of Christ.
God does not ask you to commit sin in order to demonstrate loyalty to Him.
The cross Jesus calls us to carry is not an invitation for other people to control, exploit, or destroy us.
True discipleship requires both courage and discernment.
And that brings us to a subject many people would rather avoid.
Money.
Not because money is evil.
But because money has an extraordinary ability to reveal where we place our trust.
Jesus said:
"For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." — Matthew 6:21, KJV
He did not say every person with money is unfaithful.
He did not say poverty automatically makes someone holy.
He warned about the relationship between what we treasure and where our hearts are directed.
For one person, obedience may mean becoming more generous.
For another, it may mean stopping reckless spending and faithfully providing for their family.
For someone else, it may mean refusing a dishonest opportunity that promises financial security.
And for a believer who has made comfort an idol, it may mean learning to give sacrificially and joyfully.
But never confuse the amount of a gift with the depth of a person's faith.
Jesus noticed a poor widow who gave two small coins, and He honored the extraordinary sacrifice represented by her gift (Mark 12:41–44).
Paul taught that giving should be willing rather than coerced:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
In the Greek, ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means a cheerful or glad giver.
That matters.
Because Christian generosity is not supposed to be manufactured through guilt.
Not because God loves paying supporters more than those who cannot afford to give.
But because you believe sharing biblical truth and making Christian discipleship resources accessible is a worthy mission.
What matters is that the gift is voluntary, responsible, and offered with a sincere heart.
These are simple products.
But a journal can become the place where someone writes their first honest prayer in years.
A book can become a companion during a difficult season.
A shirt can open a conversation about Jesus with someone who has never heard the Gospel clearly.
And a monthly contribution can help sustain the work behind the messages that reach people you may never meet.
The greater purpose is Christ-centered discipleship.
You are not less valuable.
You are not less faithful.
You are not outside the mission.
You can still pray, share the Gospel, encourage another believer, and help someone discover the truth of Jesus Christ.
Not because every post automatically changes a life.
Maybe someone you love has been silently drifting away from Jesus.
Maybe a friend has become comfortable with a sin that is destroying their peace.
Maybe a family member thinks they've failed God too badly to return.
Maybe someone who doesn't yet believe in Christ has never understood that Christianity is not about pretending to be good enough, but about receiving the grace of a Savior who died and rose again.
You may not know what someone is carrying behind their smile.
A shared message can become an opportunity for a conversation you never expected.
The invitation to deeper discipleship is open.
When was the last time obeying Jesus cost you something?
Because perhaps the Holy Spirit has brought a particular issue to your attention while you've been reading.
A conversation you need to have.
A sin you need to confess.
A person you need to forgive.
A compromise you need to end.
A truth you need to stop hiding from.
A responsibility you've been avoiding.
And perhaps your heart is already preparing its defense.
"But Lord, You don't understand what happened."
"But Lord, I've tried before."
"But Lord, I'm afraid."
"But Lord, what if I lose everything?"
You are speaking to the Savior who entered human suffering, endured rejection, was betrayed, and willingly went to the cross.
He understands the cost of obedience more deeply than any of us ever will.
In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed:
"Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." — Luke 22:42, KJV
He was not pretending the suffering ahead was painless.
He was not performing courage for an audience.
He was surrendering to the Father's will in the shadow of the cross.
And Philippians 2:8 tells us that Christ became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
His obedience is unlike ours.
He was sinless.
He fulfilled the Father's will perfectly.
He bore the penalty for sin as our Redeemer.
We do not repeat His saving sacrifice, and we cannot add anything to its sufficiency.
But because He died and rose again, those who belong to Him are called to walk in the newness of life He gives.
The cross is not merely a symbol to display.
It is where our Savior accomplished our redemption.
And it is the pattern of self-denying love that shapes our discipleship.
There is an important difference between a person struggling against sin and a person determined to make peace with it.
The struggling believer may stumble, grieve, confess, seek help, and return to Christ again and again.
The hardened heart begins defending what God has forbidden.
One says, "Lord, help me overcome this."
The other says, "Lord, stop confronting me about this."
One is fighting to return to the light.
The other is trying to make darkness feel comfortable.
And if you recognize yourself in that second description, don't mistake conviction for hopelessness.
God's Word exposes sin so that we will turn from it and come to Christ.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
That promise does not minimize sin.
It magnifies the faithfulness of God and the cleansing made possible through Jesus Christ.
You do not have to pretend your disobedience was harmless.
You do not have to rewrite the story to make yourself the innocent person in every chapter.
You do not have to hide behind religious language.
You can come into the light.
You can repent.
You can ask for forgiveness.
You can seek reconciliation where it is appropriate and safe.
You can make restitution where you have wronged someone.
You can take the next faithful step.
Not because you suddenly possess perfect strength.
But because the grace of Christ is sufficient to bring forgiveness and real transformation.
And perhaps that next step will cost you.
Your pride.
Your excuses.
Your comfort.
Your favorite distraction.
Your carefully maintained appearance.
Your willingness to be admired by people who do not want you to obey Jesus.
But consider what continued disobedience may already be costing you.
The dishonesty that is destroying trust.
The resentment that keeps poisoning your relationships.
The hidden sin that is becoming harder to conceal.
The compromises that are slowly reshaping your character.
The constant effort of maintaining two different versions of yourself.
One for church.
One for private life.
One that speaks about holiness.
One that secretly resists it.
And Jesus, in His mercy, calls you out of that divided existence.
Not into a life without struggles.

But into a life where your failures are no longer defended as your identity, where repentance is real, where grace is treasured, and where obedience becomes the grateful response of a heart being changed.
So here is the question I want you to carry beyond this article.
If someone could see your obedience but could not hear your Christian vocabulary, would they recognize that Jesus is the Lord you are following?
Not because perfect behavior makes someone a Christian.
But because living faith is not meant to remain invisible forever.
James 2:17 reminds us that faith without works is dead.
And Jesus said that His disciples would be recognized by their love for one another (John 13:35).
Not merely by the verses they quote.
Not merely by the causes they defend.
Not merely by the Christian content they consume.
But by the love, truth, humility, and faithfulness that increasingly mark their lives.
And now, perhaps more than anything else, you need a moment of honesty before God.
Not a performance.
Not another promise you make in the strength of your emotions.
Just an honest prayer.
"Lord Jesus, You know where I have resisted You.
You know the things I have hidden, the excuses I have made, and the places where fear has been stronger than my willingness to obey.
Forgive me for calling You Lord while refusing Your Word.
Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again.
I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my own heart apart from Your grace.
Teach me to trust You.
Give me courage to repent.
Help me obey when obedience is costly.
Show me the next faithful step, and give me strength to take it.
Not to earn Your love, but because Your love has found me.
In Jesus' name, amen."
And if this message has exposed something you have been avoiding, don't simply move on to another video, another post, another distraction.
Respond.

And if God has brought you through a season of compromise and into genuine repentance, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy. Someone reading the comments may need to know that restoration is possible.
Let the comment section become a place for encouragement, prayer, biblical truth, and honest reminders that none of us outgrows our need for Jesus.
And if these words have convicted you, save them. Return to them when you're tempted to trade long-term faithfulness for short-term comfort.
What will you do with the words of Jesus?
Because the day will come when the applause of people will mean nothing.
The numbers on your social media accounts will mean nothing.
The image you worked so hard to protect will mean nothing.
And what will matter is whether you truly belong to the Savior whose name you have been speaking.
Do not misunderstand this as a call to earn salvation by becoming impressive.
Come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Receive His grace.
Trust His finished work.
And then follow Him.
When it's joyful.
When it's ordinary.
When it's misunderstood.
When it's costly.
When you fall, return to Him.
When you're afraid, trust Him.
When you're tempted, seek His strength.
When you don't know what tomorrow holds, obey Him in what He has made clear today.
Because the goal of the Christian life is not to become someone who never needs grace.
It is to become someone whose entire life increasingly bears witness to the grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most unforgettable thing you will ever do for God will not happen on a platform, in front of a congregation, or before an audience of thousands.
Perhaps it will happen tonight.
In a quiet room.
With tears no one else sees.
When you finally open your hands and surrender the very thing you once believed you could never release.
And whisper:
"Jesus, I trust You more."
The thing you are afraid to surrender may be the very place where your heart most needs to discover that Jesus is enough.
